Example: head = [] -> []

data.reference_solution:
def reverseList(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    vals = []
    curr = head
    while curr:
        vals.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next
    vals.reverse()
    new_head = None
    curr = None
    for v in vals:
        node = ListNode(v)
        if not new_head:
            new_head = node
            curr = new_head
        else:
            curr.next = node
            curr = curr.next
    return new_head

data.key_insight: As we traverse the linked list, we can reverse the direction of the pointers by keeping track of the previous node and the current node, carefully preserving the reference to the next node before overwriting it.

steps.title: Initialize Pointers
steps.detail: Set up a previous pointer initialized to None and a current pointer initialized to the head of the list.

steps.title: Iterate and Reverse
steps.detail: While the current pointer is not None, save the next node, point the current node's next to the previous node, move previous to current, and move current to the saved next node.

steps.title: Return New Head
steps.detail: When the traversal completes, the previous pointer will be pointing at the new head of the reversed list. Return it.

data.pattern_summary: In-place pointer manipulation allows modifying structural links without allocating new memory or redundant passes.

pattern_options.name: Iterative Pointer Reversal
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We adjust the next pointers directly during a single traversal.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. A hash map stores values for fast access, but does not help restructure linear links.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. While we use multiple pointer variables, two pointers typically mean converging or sliding window setups on arrays.

pattern_options.name: Recursion with memoization
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Memoization is for overlapping subproblems with repeated calculations, which does not apply here.

signals.phrase: Given the head of a singly linked list
signals.hint: Indicates we are working with a sequential chain of nodes connected by pointers rather than an index-based array.
Implies we need to flip the direction of the connections between the nodes.

data.brute_force_idea: Collect all node values into an array, reverse the array, and construct a brand new linked list from those reversed values.
data.brute_force_why: We traverse the list once to copy values and once more to build the new nodes, resulting in linear time relative to the number of nodes.
data.bottleneck: The direct approach is already O(n) in time and O(n) in space because every node must be visited at least once to reverse the list. There is no wasted work.
bottleneck_hints: Consider how many times you must look at each node to change its direction.
Can you visit every node fewer than once if you need to touch them all?
Since every node must be processed, O(n) is the lower bound for visiting time.

data.overview: The algorithm reverses a singly linked list iteratively by maintaining three pointers: previous, current, and next. It processes each node one by one, redirecting the current node's pointer backward until the entire list is reversed.
data.intuition: Imagine walking down a path of stepping stones and turning each arrow sign around to point backward to where you came from, making sure you look at the next stone before you flip its arrow.

flow_nodes.label: Initialize Pointers
flow_nodes.detail: Set prev_node to None and current_node to head.

flow_nodes.label: Check current_node
flow_nodes.detail: Continue looping as long as current_node is not None.

flow_nodes.label: Save next_node
flow_nodes.detail: Store the reference to the next node before overwriting.

flow_nodes.label: Advance Pointers
flow_nodes.detail: Move prev_node and current_node one step forward.

flow_nodes.label: Return New Head
flow_nodes.detail: Return prev_node which is now the new head of the reversed list.

pitfalls: Forgetting to store next_node before changing current_node.next, which causes a broken link and lost nodes.
Returning head instead of prev_node at the end, which results in returning the tail of the original list.
Failing to handle the edge case of an empty list (head is None).

data.insight: The brute force approach wastes time and memory by copying all node values into an array, reversing them, and allocating an entirely new linked list. The optimized iterative solution avoids this extra storage entirely by rewiring the existing next pointers in place as you traverse the list once. Measured evidence confirms this: step counts scale linearly with n, growing from 24 steps at n=4 to 164 steps at n=32.

derivation.note: Evaluates the while loop condition until current_node becomes null.
Saves the next reference so we do not lose the rest of the list.
Reverses the pointer to point backward.
Advances current_node forward to the saved next node.
Returns the new head pointer once.

data.time_summary: Lines 3, 4, and 12 run in constant time. Lines 6 through 10 execute inside a loop that runs exactly n times. Combining these gives 5n + 3 total operations, which simplifies to O(n) time complexity.
data.space_summary: The algorithm only uses a fixed number of pointer variables (prev_node, current_node, next_node) regardless of the size of the input list. This results in O(1) auxiliary space complexity.
data.takeaway: When modifying linked lists, maintain three pointers (previous, current, next) to safely reverse pointers in place without losing track of the remaining nodes or allocating extra memory.
mistakes: Forgetting to save current_node.next before overwriting it, which orphans the rest of the linked list.
Returning head at the end instead of prev_node, which returns the original first node (now pointing to nothing or caught in a cycle) instead of the new head.
Failing to handle empty lists (head = None), though the while loop condition safely skips execution in that case.
